allspice.name: Allspice
allspice.gcms_summary: Eugenol 54–74%, β-Myrcene 10–16%, Chavicol (4-Vinylphenol) 5–12.5%, Methyl Eugenol 7–12%, β-Caryophyllene ~6.5%, D-Limonene 2–11%, 1,8-Cineole and Linalool 1–2% each. Eugenol so dominates odor activity that the others serve primarily as modifiers — the "clove + pepper + cinnamon" impression is almost entirely eugenol with caryophyllene and myrcene adding spice and depth. Guatemalan fruit EO study (PMC7597960) identified 18 compounds ≥0.1%: α-Humulene and (E)-β-Ocimene each ~1.2–1.3%; minor sesquiterpenes (α-Ylangene, δ-Amorphene, Germacrene D, γ-Muurolene, Caryophyllene oxide) and monoterpenes (Terpinen-4-ol, 1,8-Cineole, Terpinolene, γ-Terpinene) at <1% each.

basil.name: Basil (Sweet)
basil.variety: Sweet/European/Italian chemotype only. Thai, clove, and other chemotypes differ significantly (eugenol- or methyl eugenol-dominant) and require separate profiling.
basil.gcms_summary: Linalool 60–80%, Methyl chavicol (estragole) 10–25%, 1,8-Cineole 6–12%. Secondary compounds consistently present but at <5% each: Eugenol 2–10% (varies widely; trace in pure linalool types, higher in linalool+eugenol subtype), β-Caryophyllene 1–5%, (E)-β-Ocimene 1–2%, β-Myrcene and β-Pinene ~1% each, Germacrene D ~0.5–1%, Camphor ~0.3–1%. Composition varies significantly by cultivar, geography, and harvest stage.

compounds.notes: Isomerizes in acidic conditions — add any acid only after straining and cooling
Highly variable: trace in pure linalool type; up to 10% in linalool+eugenol subtype

basil.warnings: Acid caution: linalool isomerizes in acidic conditions — never add acid before straining and cooling.

black-sesame.name: Sesame Seeds (Black)
black-sesame.gcms_summary: Character defined by Maillard reaction products formed during toasting. 4-Vinylguaiacol (OAV 160) dominates the burnt-clove-smoky impression. Furaneol (OAV 80) provides caramel sweetness. 2,5-Dimethylpyrazine and alkylpyrazines (2-ethyl-6-methylpyrazine, 2,6-diethylpyrazine) deliver roasted/nutty notes. Thiazoles (2,4-dimethylthiazole, 4-methylthiazole) add coffee-roasted and meaty dimensions. 3-Methylbutanal (Strecker degradation from leucine/isoleucine) contributes high-OAV malty-fruity notes. Syringol and guaiacol provide smoky-phenolic depth from lignin degradation during roasting. 2-Furfurylthiol (threshold ~0.01 ppb) adds coffee-roasted sulfurous character. Sesamol forms from sesamolin degradation above ~180°C (356°F) and provides the characteristic earthy-phenolic sesame base note. Black vs. white: Black seeds contain statistically lower levels of 2,5-dimethylpyrazine and ethyl acetate than white sesame; overall profile is similar but black sesame reads as earthier and more bitter.

cinnamon.name: Cinnamon
cinnamon.variety: Ceylon (C. verum): (E)-Cinnamaldehyde 65–80%, Eugenol 4–5%, β-Caryophyllene 3–4%, Linalool 2–7%, (E)-Cinnamyl acetate 0.5–2.7%, 1,8-Cineole 0.8–5.4%. Cassia (C. cassia): (E)-Cinnamaldehyde 85–93%, eugenol trace. Simpler, more intensely "cinnamon," less nuance.
cinnamon.gcms_summary: Ceylon (C. verum) bark EO: (E)-Cinnamaldehyde 65–80%, β-Caryophyllene 3–6.5%, Linalool 2–7%, Eugenol 4–5%, (E)-Cinnamyl acetate 0.5–2.7%, 1,8-Cineole 0.8–5.4%, p-Cymene 1.4–1.9%, δ-Cadinene ~1.4%, D-Limonene ~1.2%, α-Humulene 0.2–1.7%, α-Pinene 0.65–1.3%, Benzyl benzoate 0.5–0.75%. Cassia (C. cassia) bark EO: Cinnamaldehyde 85–93%; nearly all other compounds at trace levels. Cassia also contains coumarin (5–16 mg/g dry bark, not present as aroma volatile), essentially absent in Ceylon.

fennel-bulb.name: Fennel (Bulb)
fennel-bulb.variety: fresh vegetable (Florence/finocchio). Trans-anethole 29–56%, D-Limonene 31–54% (co-dominant; ratio varies by cultivar, some show limonene exceeding anethole). Fenchyl acetate 2.4–7.9%, γ-Terpinene 0.7–3.4%, Estragole 0.8–1.7%, α-Pinene 0.5–2.3%, β-Myrcene 0.7–1.2%, Fenchone 0–0.8%.
fennel-bulb.gcms_summary: Trans-anethole and D-Limonene are co-dominant in fennel bulb EO across 16 cultivars (Purdue study); their ratio varies considerably and limonene can exceed anethole in some types. This contrasts with fennel seed where anethole alone is 34–83%. Fenchyl acetate (2.4–7.9%) provides a sweet fir-pine modifier. Fenchone and estragole are present but minor. trans-2-Hexenal defines the fresh green top note of the raw vegetable. Bulb yields only ~0.05% EO vs. 2–6% in seed — dramatically lower aromatic concentration per gram.

fennel-seed.name: Fennel (Seed)
fennel-seed.variety: Chemotype note: Sweet fennel (anethole-dominant cultivars): Trans-anethole 34–98%, Fenchone 4–17%, Estragole 0.2–7%, Limonene 0.3–10%, α-Pinene 2–5%. Wild/bitter fennel (subsp. piperitum): Estragole can reach 72%; anethole drops sharply. Composition varies significantly by variety and geographic origin.
fennel-seed.gcms_summary: 54 compounds identified across 12 varieties (PMC7931402). Sweet fennel is overwhelmingly anethole-dominant. Fenchone provides the bitter/camphorous modifier. Estragole adds sweet-anise complexity and is the dominant compound in wild subspecies. Minor monoterpenes (sabinene, α-pinene, β-pinene, γ-terpinene) add fresh top notes. p-Anisaldehyde and fenchyl acetate are trace but aroma-active.

fig-leaf.name: Fig (Leaf)
fig-leaf.gcms_summary: Over 121 volatile constituents identified; sesquiterpenes are the dominant class in leaves. β-Damascenone (~10%) is the key character-impact compound (rose/cooked-apple/jammy). Benzyl alcohol (~4.6%) provides sweet-floral roundness. Germacrene D, β-Caryophyllene, τ-Elemene, β-Elemene, and α-Ylangene are the major sesquiterpenes; this sesquiterpene-heavy profile is leaf-specific (differs sharply from fig fruit). trans-2-Hexenal defines the green top note. Psoralen (~10%) and Bergapten (~2%) are furanocoumarins — phototoxic, non-flavor — see warnings.

green-peas.name: Pea (Green)
green-peas.gcms_summary: 39–47 compounds identified including aldehydes, alcohols, ketones, and furans. Character defined by methoxypyrazines (IBMP, IPMP) at ultra-low thresholds — together produce the classic green pea note at ng/L concentrations. Hexanal and trans-2-hexenal are high-OAV C6 aldehydes from lipoxygenase activity on membrane lipids; blanching deactivates lipoxygenase and fixes their levels. 1-Octen-3-ol adds earthy-fungal dimension. Nonanal adds waxy-fatty-floral background. 2-Pentylfuran provides the beany-legume background note from lipid oxidation.

jasmine-tea.name: Tea (Jasmine)
jasmine-tea.variety: green tea scented with jasmine flowers
jasmine-tea.gcms_summary: 78 volatile components identified (29 terpenes, 28 esters, 6 alcohols, 8 N-containing compounds). Linalool is the dominant odorant by OAV; benzyl acetate, benzyl alcohol, methyl anthranilate, and indole are the core jasmine character contributors. Geraniol, nerolidol, and eugenol are secondary floral and spicy-depth modifiers. α-Farnesene and (Z)-3-hexenyl benzoate are additional floral-green ester contributors. Short-chain aldehydes (BP 64–93°C / 147–199°F) are essentially fully lost in warm brewing.

lemongrass.name: Lemongrass
lemongrass.gcms_summary: Geranial (α-citral) 36–41%, Neral (β-citral) 28–34%, β-Myrcene 14–17%, Geraniol 2–6%, D-Limonene 1–5%, Linalool ~1–2%. Citral (neral + geranial combined) accounts for 70–85% of the essential oil.

compounds.notes: ~1–2%; minor floral modifier

lemongrass.warnings: Acid caution: citral undergoes acid-catalyzed cyclization to off-flavor monoterpenes (p-cymene, p-cresol) — never add acidic ingredients until the infused cream is strained and cooled.

litsea-cubeba.name: Litsea Cubeba
litsea-cubeba.gcms_summary: Geranial 44–50%, Neral 34–37%, Citral combined 78–87%, Citronellal 0.6–6.2% (variable by region/chemotype), D-Limonene 0.7–5.3%, Linalool 1.2–1.6%, Geraniol ~1.1%. Sensory character: sweet, fresh lemon-citral, green, grassy, slightly fruity — sweeter and less herbal than lemongrass due to lower myrcene content.

litsea-cubeba.warnings: Same acid caution as lemongrass: citral and citronellal undergo acid-catalyzed cyclization — no acid before straining and cooling.

lychee.name: Lychee
lychee.gcms_summary: AEDA of fresh lychee (PMC9322243) identified 31 key odorants. Methional (FD 1024) is highest-FD compound; geraniol (FD 512) and furaneol (FD 128) follow. Nerol (FD 64) contributes softer rose-floral notes alongside geraniol; (E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal (FD 32) adds a green-cucumber dimension; nerolidol (FD 32) provides a woody-floral base. Citronellol and linalool are lower-FD but aroma-active. cis-Rose oxide is the defining character compound (highest OAV; only the (−)-cis isomer is odor-active at ~0.5 ppb threshold). β-Damascenone was not detected in this study.

nutmeg.name: Nutmeg
nutmeg.gcms_summary: Sabinene 10–50%, α-Pinene 7–20%, β-Pinene 5–15%, γ-Terpinene 5–15%, Terpinen-4-ol 5–18%, Myristicin 5–15%, Eugenol 0–18% (highly variable; mean ~7%), Elemicin 1–3%, β-Myrcene 1–5%, α-Terpineol 1–3%, α-Terpinene <2%, Linalool trace–2%. Oil divides into ~88% monoterpenes and ~12% phenylpropanoids. Myristicin is the character-defining phenylpropanoid; elemicin and eugenol co-contribute the spice-clove notes.

oolong-tea.name: Tea (Oolong)
oolong-tea.gcms_summary: Key odorants by OAV: Nerolidol (OAV 108–184), Indole (OAV 96–138), Linalool (OAV 63–87), β-Damascenone (OAV 29–59), Geraniol (floral backbone). Short-chain aldehydes (2-methylpropanal, 3-methylbutanal) have very high OAVs but boiling points of 64–93°C — they volatilize in any warm infusion. Phenylacetaldehyde (Strecker aldehyde) contributes honey-rose-hyacinth character. Methyl salicylate is a signature compound of Dancong/Wuyi styles. Phenethyl alcohol adds rose-honey body. The persistent floral-fruity character is defined by nerolidol, linalool, damascenone, and indole.

pea-shoots.name: Pea (Shoot)
pea-shoots.gcms_summary: IBMP and IPMP are the character-defining green pea methoxypyrazines at ppt concentrations (IBMP threshold ~2 ppt). Hexanal (high-OAV, enzymatic), trans-2-Hexenal, and cis-3-hexenol (leaf alcohol) form the sharp green/grassy top notes — all C6 lipoxygenase products. 1-Octen-3-ol adds mushroom-earthy depth. Nonanal and 2-pentyl-furan contribute secondary green-beany notes. Lipoxygenase in raw shoots generates additional hexanal and hexenol on cell damage; blanching deactivates this enzyme.

sichuan-peppercorn.name: Peppercorn (Sichuan)
sichuan-peppercorn.variety: dried red pericarp. Variety note: Green peppercorn (young Z. bungeanum or Z. schinifolium) is linalool/limonene-dominant (citrus-forward); mature red (dried Z. bungeanum) is linalyl acetate/myrcene-dominant (floral-herbal) with higher sanshool content.
sichuan-peppercorn.gcms_summary: Linalool is the dominant odorant (OAV 10–223 across varieties), with D-Limonene (OAV 28–167) and β-Myrcene (OAV 24–129) as strong secondary contributors. Linalyl Acetate (OAV 6–121) more pronounced in red varieties. Geraniol, geranyl acetate, terpinen-4-ol, sabinene, and β-Pinene are documented secondary EO constituents across 40–100+ compounds identified by GC-MS. (E,E)-2,4-Decadienal carries the highest measured OAV (1163–2015) but is primarily generated by thermal oxidation at ≥130°C — absent in cold or warm (<80°C) infusions.

sugar-snap-peas.gcms_summary: Essentially the same primary volatiles as pea shoots: IBMP and IPMP drive the methoxypyrazine character; hexanal, trans-2-hexenal, cis-3-hexenol, and 1-octen-3-ol define the green/mushroom backdrop. The pod adds 2-pentyl-furan (beany-earthy) and higher relative IPMP. Nonanal and hexanol are secondary lipoxygenase products. Lipoxygenase in raw pods generates additional hexanal on cell damage — blanch to deactivate.

saffron.name: Saffron
saffron.variety: dried stigmas (threads). Quality is graded by ISO 3632 using three absorbance values: crocin (color/Style I ≥200), picrocrocin (bitterness/≥70), safranal (aroma/20–50). Higher-grade saffron has proportionally more of all three.
saffron.gcms_summary: Safranal dominates the volatile fraction (up to 70%) and is the primary aroma compound; it forms during drying via hydrolysis of the glycoside picrocrocin. Lanierone (2-hydroxy-4,4,6-trimethyl-2,5-cyclohexadien-1-one) has the highest flavor dilution factor. 4-Ketoisophorone is a documented secondary volatile with earthy-herbaceous character. Picrocrocin (~4% dry weight) is the primary bitter taste compound and safranal precursor. Crocin (6–16% dry weight) provides color. Minor volatiles include linalool, geraniol, and β-ionone. Fresh stigmas are nearly odorless; the characteristic saffron flavor develops during the drying process.

sumac.name: Sumac
sumac.variety: dried ground fruit (spice). Volatile profile varies significantly by geographic origin; Palestinian sumac is α-pinene-dominant, Egyptian is cymene/limonene-forward. The non-volatile acid and tannin content defines the characteristic flavor and is more consistent across origins.
sumac.gcms_summary: 74–263 volatile compounds identified across origins. Sesquiterpene hydrocarbons are the dominant volatile class (40–58% of fresh fruit), followed by monoterpene hydrocarbons (17–34%). Key volatiles: α-pinene, (E)-β-caryophyllene, nonanal, p-anisaldehyde. However, the characteristic culinary flavor of sumac is defined primarily by non-volatile compounds: malic acid (3–5% dry weight; dominant organic acid) and gallotannins (~4% dry weight; astringency). The volatile terpenes provide a secondary aromatic backdrop. Upon roasting, furfural and nonanal become enriched (up to 34.3% and significantly elevated respectively).

pineapple.name: Pineapple
pineapple.variety: fresh or frozen pulp. Variety note: OAV rankings shift by cultivar — ethyl 2-methylbutanoate dominates in many commercial types (OAV up to 3707); furaneol dominates in others (OAV up to 2549). Both are always present and together define the recognizable pineapple character.
pineapple.gcms_summary: Nearly 480 volatiles identified; ~40 contribute meaningfully. Esters dominate (84% of volatiles), followed by lactones and terpenes. The character is defined by two compounds: ethyl 2-methylbutanoate (fruity-fresh top note) and furaneol (caramel-sweet body note). Allyl hexanoate is a highly characteristic pineapple ester; methyl 2-methylbutanoate is the methyl analogue of the dominant ester. Ethyl hexanoate, δ-octalactone, γ-octalactone, methyl hexanoate, ethyl butanoate, decanal, and ethyl 3-(methylthio)propanoate are secondary modifiers.

pineapple.warnings: Bromelain caution: raw pineapple juice contains bromelain (a cysteine protease) that degrades gelatin, egg proteins, and dairy proteins. Do not add raw juice to a custard base or any gelatin-set preparation — the proteins will fail to set. Heat-treat (>70°C for 5+ min) or use commercially pasteurized juice/concentrate to deactivate. Ethyl 2-methylbutanoate is extremely volatile — any heated extraction will lose the top note; blend cold pineapple puree in after cooking and cooling.

almond-extract.name: Almond (Extract)
almond-extract.scientific_name: Prunus dulcis var. amara (bitter almond) or Prunus armeniaca / P. persica (apricot/peach kernel)
almond-extract.variety: Commercial extract = benzaldehyde dissolved in food-grade ethanol (~32–35% alcohol). Source material is bitter almond, apricot kernel, or peach pit — all rich in amygdalin, which hydrolyzes to benzaldehyde + HCN; HCN is removed in processing. Imitation extract uses synthetic benzaldehyde.
almond-extract.gcms_summary: Benzaldehyde dominates (~63–90% of volatile fraction depending on source material and method). Benzyl alcohol is a secondary smoothing note (~1–10%). Benzoic acid (~15% of bitter almond essential oil) is the third major constituent. Benzyl benzoate is a high-boiling fixative present in bitter almond oil; linalool is a trace floral background note. The alcohol carrier in commercial extract (ethanol) is not a flavor compound but significantly affects how benzaldehyde disperses in a dairy base.

vanilla-bean.name: Vanilla (Bean)
vanilla-bean.variety: Cured bean (Madagascar/Bourbon, Mexican, or Indonesian). Tahitian vanilla (V. tahitensis) has a distinctly different profile with prominent anisaldehyde and anisyl alcohol and requires separate profiling.
vanilla-bean.gcms_summary: Vanillin dominates (~70–85% of the phenolic fraction by weight in cured beans) and is the single most aroma-active compound. p-Hydroxybenzaldehyde is the second most abundant phenolic — sweet and floral. Vanillic acid and guaiacol are minor by mass but high in aroma significance; guaiacol and 4-methylguaiacol (creosol) provide the smoky-woody phenolic depth that distinguishes natural vanilla from synthetic vanillin. Coumarin and eugenol contribute tonka-spice modulation. Vanillyl alcohol and p-anisaldehyde are minor sweet-phenolic notes; benzaldehyde is trace. Over 200 volatiles identified total; profile varies significantly by curing method and origin.

green-cardamom.name: Cardamom (Green)
green-cardamom.variety: dried seed pods (inner seeds). Ratio of α-terpinyl acetate to 1,8-cineole varies by geographic origin — some studies show cineole-dominant (55%:29%); others show terpinyl acetate-dominant (46%:26%). Use freshly ground seeds; husk contributes far less oil than the seeds.
green-cardamom.gcms_summary: α-Terpinyl acetate and 1,8-cineole together account for 75–85% of the essential oil; their ratio is origin-dependent (see variety note). α-Terpinyl acetate (28–46%) provides the characteristic sweet floral cardamom note; 1,8-cineole (26–55%) adds eucalyptus cooling character. Minor contributors: terpinen-4-ol ~3%, α-terpineol ~3%, D-limonene ~2.5%, linalool ~1–4%, sabinene ~1–2%, β-pinene ~1–2%, neryl acetate ~1%, methyl eugenol ~0.5%, linalyl acetate ~0.5%.

wasabi.name: Wasabi (Root)
wasabi.gcms_summary: AITC (primary pungent volatile), 3-BITC (secondary pungent), 6-MSITC (sweet-vegetable complexity unique to real wasabi), and PEITC (minor peppery note from gluconasturtiin). All are enzymatically generated (not pre-formed): myrosinase enzyme, released on cell damage, converts glucosinolate precursors to isothiocyanates. Non-ITC volatiles identified in wasabi are minor trace aliphatics (hexanal, nonanal) with no meaningful aroma contribution relative to the ITCs.

coconut.name: Coconut
coconut.gcms_summary: Lactones dominate the characteristic coconut note (delta-octalactone, delta-decalactone, gamma-nonalactone). In coconut milk, esters (ethyl decanoate, ethyl octanoate) account for ~60% of volatiles by relative area, lactones ~29%. Aldehydes (nonanal, octanal) add fatty-fresh top notes. Percentage figures are relative abundances in raw coconut milk headspace; lactone absolute concentrations are low but well above odor thresholds.

cucumber.name: Cucumber
cucumber.gcms_summary: (E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal and (E)-2-nonenal together account for >80% of the perceived aroma impact (by relative concentration in headspace). Both are C9 aldehydes derived from linolenic acid via the lipoxygenase pathway. C6 lipoxygenase products (hexanal, cis-3-hexenol, trans-2-hexenal) add green/grassy freshness. Nonanal and octanal provide waxy-fatty background; (E,E)-2,4-heptadienal is a minor fresh-fatty contributor.

coffee-bean.name: Coffee (Bean)
coffee-bean.variety: Arabica or Robusta; roast level shifts compound ratios significantly
coffee-bean.gcms_summary: Roasted coffee contains 800–1000+ identified volatiles. 2-Furfurylthiol is the single most impactful compound (OAV 100s–1000s; threshold 0.01 ppb). Furaneol, guaiacol, and 4-vinylguaiacol contribute caramel and smoky-phenolic dimensions. Multiple pyrazines (2,5-dimethylpyrazine, trimethylpyrazine, 2-ethyl-5-methylpyrazine) provide the roasty-nutty-earthy character — all increase with darker roast. Phenylacetaldehyde (Strecker of phenylalanine) adds honey-rose character. 3-Methylbutanal (Strecker of leucine) adds malty notes but is largely lost in hot preparations. Furfural contributes caramel-almond roast notes. Beta-damascenone is a trace but impactful fruity modifier. Methional is heat-labile and largely absent from cooked preparations.

coriander-seed.name: Coriander (Seed)
coriander-seed.gcms_summary: Linalool is overwhelmingly dominant (56–75% of essential oil) — the seed is essentially a linalool delivery vehicle with supporting terpene complexity. Camphor (~2%), α-Pinene (~3–5%), and linalyl acetate (~2%) provide medicinal, piney, and floral-woody secondary character. γ-Terpinene (~5–10%) and β-Pinene (~2–4%) add citrus-herbal and fresh-woody support. p-Cymene (~2%), terpinen-4-ol (~2%), geraniol (~1%), and d-limonene (~2%) round out the profile.

coriander-leaf.name: Coriander (Leaf)
coriander-leaf.gcms_summary: Completely different profile from the seed. C10–C12 alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehydes define the characteristic soapy-citrus-coriander aroma (and are responsible for the 'soapy' perception in genetic non-tasters). (E)-2-Decenal is the dominant volatile by mass; (E)-2-Dodecenal has the highest character-impact by GC-olfactometry. Linalool is present (12–30%) and contributes floral lift. Beta-ionone and eugenol are trace character-impact odorants. In fresh leaf headspace, (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate (~70%) dominates as a handling artifact but (Z/E)-decenal isomers drive the recognizable cilantro smell.

thai-basil.name: Basil (Thai)
thai-basil.variety: Estragole + citral chemotype. Distinct from sweet basil (linalool-dominant) and holy basil (eugenol-dominant). Eugenol and methyl eugenol absent or trace.
thai-basil.gcms_summary: Estragole (methyl chavicol, 60–80%) is the dominant compound; geranial and neral (citral, ~10–25% combined) are the major secondary contributors producing a lemon-anise profile. β-Caryophyllene (~3–5%) is a minor woody note. Linalool (2–5%), β-myrcene (~2%), (E)-β-ocimene (~1%), and trace eugenol round out the profile. The estragole + citral combination is the defining chemotype — distinct from all other Ocimum varieties used in cooking.

Profile differs fundamentally from sweet basil (linalool) and Thai basil (estragole+citral).

ginger.name: Ginger
ginger.variety: Fresh rhizome; dried/processed ginger has significantly different volatile profile
ginger.gcms_summary: Sesquiterpenes dominate: zingiberene (~18–30%) is the signature compound; β-sesquiphellandrene (~10–15%) and ar-curcumene (~5–8%) contribute woody-spicy warmth. Monoterpenoid aldehydes (geranial ~8%, neral ~5%) deliver the lemon-citrus brightness; 1,8-cineole (~7%) adds cooling eucalyptus; camphene (~9%) gives piney camphor. Geraniol, nerolidol, and citronellal are secondary contributors. Linalool, β-myrcene, β-phellandrene, and α-pinene round out the profile at low levels. OAV data: geranial and neral are highest-impact aroma compounds despite lower abundance than zingiberene (which has high OAV threshold).

banana.name: Banana
banana.variety: Commercial Cavendish. Profile here reflects FlavorDB entity 167 (87 compounds) supplemented with GC-MS literature.
banana.gcms_summary: Ester-dominated profile. Isoamyl acetate is the dominant volatile in ripe Cavendish banana (~5–30% of headspace by GC-MS) and the defining character compound — its absence from FlavorDB entity 167 is a data gap, not absence from the fruit. Isoamyl butyrate, isoamyl propanoate, and butyl acetate round out the ester suite; ethyl butanoate provides fresh top note; isopentyl hexanoate and isoamyl isovalerate add tropical fruit body. Isoamyl alcohol is the fusel alcohol backbone from which most banana esters are biosynthetically derived. Eugenol, hexanal, and trans-2-hexenal contribute minor complexity in ripe fruit; 2-heptanone adds musty undertone.

white-nectarine.name: White Nectarine
white-nectarine.gcms_summary: White-fleshed nectarines are characterized by higher total volatile content and elevated levels of phenols and terpenes compared to yellow-fleshed cultivars. Food Sci. Tech. 2023) provide the basis for this profile.

corn.name: Corn (Sweet Corn / Maize)
corn.variety: sweet corn (Zea mays var. saccharata/rugosa); profile below is dominated by cooked/heat-generated compounds, with raw lipid-oxidation volatiles as a secondary layer
corn.gcms_summary: Dimethyl sulfide (DMS) is the primary aroma-impact compound of cooked sweet corn, giving the characteristic sweet, creamed/canned-corn note; it forms during heating from a non-volatile precursor and is essentially absent raw. Hydrogen sulfide, methanethiol, and ethanethiol are secondary sulfur volatiles with very low odor thresholds that reinforce the cooked-corn character. Acetaldehyde and ethanol are also abundant in cooked corn headspace. Separately, raw and minimally processed corn carries a lipid-oxidation-derived aldehyde/furan profile: hexanal, trans-2-octenal, nonanal, trans-2-nonenal, and decanal (sweet-floral and fatty notes), plus 1-octen-3-ol and 2-pentylfuran (green-bean, earthy, mushroom notes). All of these together define corn's dual character: green/raw vegetal on the fresh cob, sulfurous-sweet once cooked.

corn.warnings: DMS, H2S, methanethiol, ethanethiol, and acetaldehyde are all gases or near-gases at room temperature — an open-pot simmer or steep will lose nearly all of the characteristic cooked-corn sulfur aroma. tarragon.name: Tarragon
tarragon.variety: French tarragon (estragole-dominant, culinary standard) vs. Russian tarragon (higher thujone/camphor, more bitter/less sweet-anise) - profile below reflects French tarragon unless noted
tarragon.gcms_summary: Estragole (methyl chavicol) is overwhelmingly dominant (60-75% of essential oil in French tarragon), giving the characteristic sweet anise/licorice flavor. Ocimene, elemicin, and limonene are notable secondary terpenes. A broad monoterpene background (sabinene, alpha/beta-pinene, myrcene, gamma-terpinene, alpha/beta-phellandrene, camphene, p-cymene, 3-carene, linalool, eucalyptol) contributes green-herbaceous-piney depth. Genus-marker Artemisia ketones (artemisia ketone, alpha-thujone, D-camphor) are present at low levels in French tarragon, much higher in Russian tarragon and other Artemisia species. Coumarin and dihydrocoumarin give a hay-like background note characteristic of dried tarragon. cis-3-Hexenal, trans-2/3-hexenol, and cis-3-hexenyl acetate contribute fresh-cut-grass green-leaf top notes. white-peach.gcms_summary: Shares the core peach lactone/aldehyde profile with yellow-fleshed peach (gamma/delta-decalactone, hexanal, trans-2-hexenal, benzaldehyde, 1-hexanol) but is distinguished by furan and ether volatiles found exclusively in white-fleshed fruit: linalool oxide, 2-pentylfuran, and theaspirane. black-peppercorn.name: Peppercorn (Black)
black-peppercorn.variety: dried whole unripe berry, sun-dried with skin intact (the skin darkens and contributes tannin/phenolic depth absent in white pepper)
black-peppercorn.gcms_summary: Piperine is the defining pungency compound - a non-volatile alkaloid responsible for black pepper's characteristic heat/bite, essentially odorless itself but the primary taste-active flavor compound. Beta-caryophyllene is the dominant aroma sesquiterpene (often 20-40% of the essential oil), giving warm, woody, slightly peppery depth. A very broad monoterpene background (limonene, sabinene, alpha/beta-pinene, beta-myrcene, delta-3-carene, alpha/beta-phellandrene, gamma-terpinene, camphene, p-cymene, terpinolene, eucalyptol) contributes fresh, piney, citrus-green top notes characteristic of freshly cracked pepper. Terpene alcohols (linalool, terpinen-4-ol, alpha-terpineol, borneol, D-camphor, cedrol, citronellol) and sesquiterpene alcohols (spathulenol, nerolidol, farnesol) add floral-woody depth. Minor phenylpropanoids (eugenol, methyleugenol, isoeugenol, safrole) and phenolics (carvacrol, thymol) contribute clove-spice complexity shared with many other spices.

white-peppercorn.name: Peppercorn (White)
white-peppercorn.variety: same species/berry as black pepper, but harvested fully ripe and processed by retting (soaking in water for ~1-2 weeks to ferment and loosen the skin, which is then rubbed off before drying) - the fermentation step is what distinguishes its VOC profile from black pepper
white-peppercorn.gcms_summary: Shares black pepper's core pungency compound, piperine, and a reduced version of its terpene background (limonene, sabinene, beta-myrcene, alpha-phellandrene, eucalyptol, eugenol) - reduced because the retting/soaking process leaches out some volatile terpenes that survive intact in whole sun-dried black peppercorns. The defining difference is a set of fermentation-derived compounds produced by microbial activity during retting: 3-methylindole (skatole, a fecal-at-high/floral-at-trace compound), and short-chain fatty acids (hexanoic, valeric, butyric, isovaleric acids) that give white pepper its characteristic "barnyard"/fermented, slightly cheesy-goaty undertone beneath the shared pepper-terpene top notes. This is why white pepper reads as muskier and less bright than black pepper despite coming from the same fruit.

bay-leaf.name: Bay Leaf
bay-leaf.variety: Mediterranean / Turkish bay (Laurus nobilis). California bay (Umbellularia californica) is a different species dominated by umbellulone and is far more aggressive — not interchangeable. Indian bay leaf (Cinnamomum tamala) is cinnamon-family and also not interchangeable.
bay-leaf.gcms_summary: Overwhelmingly monoterpenoid: monoterpenes make up 95–99% of the volatile oil. 1,8-Cineole (eucalyptol) dominates at 43.9–65.5% and defines the eucalyptus-camphoraceous character. alpha-Terpinyl acetate is the consistent second compound at 10–18%, contributing the sweet herbal-floral lift that distinguishes bay from pure eucalyptus. Sabinene, alpha- and beta-pinene, myrcene, limonene, alpha-thujene and the terpinenes form the piney-green top note. Linalool, terpinen-4-ol, alpha-terpineol and sabinene hydrate add soft floral-woody body. The phenylpropanoid fraction is small by mass but high in aroma impact: eugenol, methyleugenol, eugenyl acetate and elemicin give the clove-warm spice edge. beta-Caryophyllene, beta-elemene and spathulenol are the main sesquiterpenes. Composition varies substantially with season, origin and whether the sample is food- or pharmaceutical-grade. VOC profile cross-referenced against FlavorDB entity 305 (Laurel).

hazelnut.name: Hazelnut
hazelnut.variety: Turkish (Tombul) and Italian (Tonda Gentile delle Langhe) are the standard confectionery varieties. Raw and roasted are effectively two different ingredients aromatically — the roast-generated pyrazine and pyrroline fraction does not exist in the raw nut.
hazelnut.gcms_summary: Hazelnut aroma is carried by a small number of very low-threshold compounds rather than a large volatile mass. Filbertone (5-methyl-(E)-2-hepten-4-one) is the character-impact compound, with an odor threshold near 0.05 ug/L and an intense nutty-roasted note; its concentration rises roughly 80% on roasting or boiling versus the raw nut. 3-Methyl-4-heptanone is the other key ketone odorant. Roasting adds the whole Maillard fraction: 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline (popcorn-roasty), 2,3-diethyl-5-methylpyrazine and related alkylpyrazines (roasted-earthy), 2-furfurylthiol (coffee-sulfury), and the Strecker aldehydes 2- and 3-methylbutanal. Homofuraneol contributes caramellic sweetness. Lipid oxidation supplies hexanal, heptanal and octanal — pleasant green-fatty at low levels and the first marker of rancidity at high ones. Benzaldehyde, phenylacetaldehyde, 2-phenylethanol and vanillin round out the sweet-floral edge; 2,3-butanedione adds buttery lift. kaffir-lime-leaf.name: Kaffir Lime Leaf (Makrut Lime Leaf)
kaffir-lime-leaf.variety: Fresh double-lobed leaf is the reference material. Dried leaf loses most of the sabinene/pinene top note and reads flatter and more soapy-rosy; frozen fresh leaf retains the profile far better than dried. Note that the leaf and the fruit peel of the same plant are aromatically different — peel oil is limonene/beta-pinene dominant, the leaf is citronellal dominant.
kaffir-lime-leaf.gcms_summary: Unusually lopsided for a citrus material: citronellal alone accounts for 61–85% of the leaf oil across studies (most reports cluster 77–85%), which is why makrut leaf smells nothing like lime fruit. Citronellol is the consistent second compound at 3.4–10.6%, adding rosy-floral sweetness. Linalool (1.9–4.9%), sabinene (~4.8%), citronellyl acetate (~1.7%), 3-carene (up to 6.6%) and beta-myrcene (~1.2%) fill out the profile. Isopulegol is present and increases with heat and acid, since it forms by cyclisation of citronellal. Minor monoterpenes (limonene, alpha- and beta-pinene, gamma-terpinene, terpinolene, p-cymene), terpene alcohols (terpinen-4-ol, alpha-terpineol, nerol, geraniol), esters (geranyl and neryl acetate) and traces of neral/geranial and beta-caryophyllene complete it. The oil is almost entirely monoterpenoid with very little sesquiterpene mass. Composition varies with growing location, leaf age and extraction method. Not present in FlavorDB; profile assembled from GC-MS literature.

compounds.notes: Overwhelmingly dominant, 61–85%; the entire character of the ingredient; LogP ~3.5 so it partitions almost exclusively into fat, essentially nothing into water
Consistent second compound, 3.4–10.6%; rosy-floral sweetness that keeps citronellal from reading as insect repellent
Reported up to 6.6% in some samples; sweet-piney; highly variable by origin
~4.8%; fresh peppery-green top note; volatile, first thing lost in an open pot
1.9–4.9%; floral-soft, rounds the citronellal edge
~1.7%; fruity-rosy ester, softer than citronellal; hydrolyses toward citronellol under long acidic heat
~1.2%; balsamic-green; volatile
Minty-cooling; forms from citronellal by acid-catalysed cyclisation, so it accumulates during long or acidic steeping — a marker of overextraction
Minor in the leaf despite dominating the fruit peel; citrus lift; volatile and prone to oxidation
Minor piney top note; BP 155°C (311°F), highly volatile
Minor woody-resinous
Minor herbal-citrus
Minor sweet pine
Minor dry-woody; rises in dried or aged leaf
Woody-earthy; hydrolysis product, increases with steeping time
Lilac-floral; also accumulates with prolonged heat
Sweet rose; supports the citronellol floral character
Sweet rose, sharper than nerol
Sweet fruity-floral ester; minor
Sweet floral ester; minor
Trace; lemon-sharp; volatile and acid-sensitive
Trace; lemon-sharp, the stronger citral isomer; volatile and acid-sensitive
Main sesquiterpene, small mass; peppery-woody base; non-volatile at custard temps

kaffir-lime-leaf.warnings: Leaves are leathery and stay fibrous no matter how long they cook — steep whole or bruised and strain them out; never blend them into a base or you get green flecks and a bitter, chlorophyll-vegetal edge. Citronellal is soapy at high concentration and the leaf is potent, so overdosing is easy. Prolonged or acidic hot steeping cyclises citronellal to isopulegol and shifts the profile from bright citrus-floral toward minty-medicinal. Do not substitute lime peel, lime zest or lime juice — different species part, different dominant compound, completely different result.

blackberry.name: Blackberry
blackberry.gcms_summary: VOC profile from FlavorDB (entity_id: 222), 150 molecules, cross-checked against SPME-GC-MS aroma literature. Blackberry has no single character-impact compound; the aroma is an accord. The high-impact odorants repeatedly named are beta-damascenone and beta-ionone (norisoprenoids, jammy/violet, trace level but very low thresholds), furaneol and homofuraneol plus mesifurane (caramel-sweet jam notes, heat-generated), linalool (floral lift), and the C6 lipoxygenase products hexanal and cis-3-hexenal with trans-2-hexen-1-ol (green, raw-crushed-fruit). Ripening shifts the profile: cis-3-hexen-1-ol and green C6 notes dominate the green stage, hexyl acetate and 2-heptanol the red stage, ketones such as 2-heptanone and 2-undecanone plus the lactones (gamma-undecalactone, gamma-dodecalactone) the fully ripe fruit. Most of the impact odorants are lipophilic (LogP 3-4), so a dairy or cream base extracts them far better than water.

compounds.notes: Homofuraneol; caramel-sweet berry-jam note, generated and intensified by heat.
Almond/marzipan note, present with trace hydrogen cyanide from seed glycosides.
Sherry/burnt-sugar note characteristic of ripe Rubus and Fragaria fruit.
Green/unripe note from lipoxygenase action on cut fruit; increases sharply when berries are crushed raw. Blanching or rapid heating suppresses it.
Character-impact odorant of ripe blackberry despite trace concentration; extremely low odor threshold, contributes the cooked-fruit/jammy top note.
Trace; supports the sweet-creamy end of the profile.
Violet-woody note; low threshold, survives pasteurisation intact.
Same lipoxygenase origin as hexanal; very unstable, dominant in raw crushed berries.
Green-leafy note of under-ripe fruit.
Sweet-fruity ester of red-to-ripe stage berries.
Peach-creamy lactone; fat-soluble, extracts preferentially into cream.
Creamy-peach lactone, reinforces dairy body.
Trace, from cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin) in the seeds. Not a hazard at culinary quantities but avoid milling seeds.
Solventy-fruity; rises sharply in over-ripe or fermenting fruit.
Fruity ketone reported in the ripe-fruit fraction.
Reported as a high-impact blackberry odorant in the aroma literature (not listed in the FlavorDB entity); floral lift, declines as fruit over-ripens.
Reported as a high-impact blackberry odorant in the aroma literature (not in the FlavorDB entity); caramelised strawberry-jam sweetness, intensifies with heat.

blackberry.warnings: Seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin) that release trace hydrogen cyanide when crushed - harmless at culinary scale but do not mill or blend the seeds aggressively. Anthocyanin colour is pH-sensitive and shifts from red-purple to blue-grey in a neutral dairy base; a small acid addition holds the colour. Fresh puree carries active enzymes, so hold cold or heat quickly to control green hexanal development.

italian-parsley.name: Italian Parsley
italian-parsley.gcms_summary: VOC profile from FlavorDB (entity_id: 338, Parsley), 167 molecules, refined with flat-leaf-specific essential oil literature. The flat-leaf variety differs sharply from curly parsley: 1,3,8-p-menthatriene (p-mentha-1,3,8-triene), the defining parsley odorant, runs about 10x higher and can reach 38-48% of leaf essential oil depending on harvest timing. The other dominant leaf-oil constituents are beta-phellandrene (~10-17%), p,alpha-dimethylstyrene, beta-myrcene, and the phenylpropanoids apiole (reported at 33-53% in flat-leaf samples) and myristicin (sometimes absent in flat-leaf chemotypes). Supporting notes come from terpinolene, alpha- and gamma-terpinene, p-cymene, sabinene, beta-caryophyllene and other sesquiterpenes, the trace galbanum-green odorant 1,3,5-undecatriene, and celery-type phthalides (sedanenolide, butylphthalide). Green cut-leaf notes (cis-3-hexenal, cis-3-hexen-1-ol, trans-2-hexenal) are lipoxygenase products formed on chopping. The profile splits cleanly by volatility: the monoterpene fraction that reads as fresh parsley is heat-labile and lost above roughly 60-70°C (140-158°F), while the phenylpropanoid and sesquiterpene fraction is fat-soluble and heat-stable and reads warm, spicy, and anise-adjacent.

compounds.notes: Fresh piney-herbal terpene, heat-labile.
Trace galbanum-green odorant with a very low threshold; contributes the fresh-crushed-leaf impression.
Celery-lovage phthalide, same savoury family as sedanenolide.
Woody-peppery sesquiterpene; strongly fat-soluble and heat-stable, persists where the monoterpenes do not.
Minor phenylpropanoid, dill-spicy; tracks with apiole.
Celery-type phthalide; contributes the savoury edge that separates parsley from purely green herbs.
Lipoxygenase-derived green note released on chopping or bruising the leaf.
Furocoumarin. Phototoxic in quantity (parsley is a known cause of phytophotodermatitis on skin contact plus UV); irrelevant at eating quantities but relevant when handling large volumes of leaf.
Non-volatile polyacetylene; source of the bitter edge in over-extracted parsley.
Second phenylpropanoid; sometimes absent in flat-leaf chemotypes. Same dose caution as apiole.
Phenylpropanoid, can be 33-53% of flat-leaf parsley leaf oil; warm sweet-phenolic backbone of parsley flavor. Strongly fat-soluble, heat-stable. Toxic at high dose - see ingredient warnings.
Major flat-leaf parsley terpene (~10-17% of leaf oil); fresh peppery-citrus, volatile and heat-labile.

The defining flat-leaf parsley odorant. Flat-leaf (Italian) parsley carries roughly 10x the level found in curly parsley, and it can reach ~40-48% of leaf essential oil at optimum harvest. Highly volatile terpene hydrocarbon: lost rapidly with heat and oxidation, so cold or brief warm infusion only.
Cut-grass green alcohol, formed on damage to the leaf.
Woody-terpenic; oxidation product of the monoterpenes, rises in dried or aged leaf.
Green-balsamic top note; the most volatile of the parsley monoterpenes, gone quickly with heat.
One of the abundant leaf-oil terpenoids of flat-leaf parsley; citrus-herbal.

italian-parsley.warnings: Apiole and myristicin are toxic in concentrated doses (hepatotoxic, and apiole is a known abortifacient and uterine stimulant); parsley leaf at culinary quantities is safe, but do not use parsley essential oil or heavily concentrated extracts, and avoid concentrated preparations in pregnancy. The leaf also contains furocoumarins (methoxsalen/xanthotoxin, bergapten) which can cause phytophotodermatitis on skin contact followed by sun exposure - wear gloves when handling large volumes. Over-extraction pulls bitter polyacetylenes (falcarindiol) and chlorophyll, giving a vegetal, grassy bitterness.

shiso.name: Shiso
shiso.variety: Red/purple shiso (akajiso) assumed as default culinary form; green shiso (aojiso) noted where it differs
shiso.gcms_summary: Perilla splits into two sharply different volatile chemotypes, and the split tracks leaf colour. GC-MS metabolomic comparison of Perillae Folium found every purple sample was the PA (perillaldehyde) chemotype and every green sample was the PK (perilla ketone) chemotype. Purple/red shiso: perillaldehyde 31.72 ± 3.12%, shisool 5.41 ± 0.86%, D-limonene 5.12 ± 1.23%. Green perilla/egoma: perilla ketone 27.50 ± 3.01%, with isoegomaketone also elevated; one cultivar study reported perilla ketone as high as 80.76% of the essential oil. Seven marker compounds separate the two: limonene, shisool and perillaldehyde run high in purple; perilla ketone, isoegomaketone, tocopheryl and squalene run high in green. Across accessions 142 volatile compounds have been identified, spanning nine chemical classes (alcohols, aldehydes, benzodioxoles, esters, ethers, ketones, monoterpenes, phenylpropanoids, sesquiterpenes); GC-olfactometry sniffing tests picked out methyl benzoate and limonene as predominant perceived odorants in one variety. beta-Caryophyllene is the consistent sesquiterpene backbone in both chemotypes.

compounds.notes: Dominant in red/purple shiso and the compound responsible for the signature cumin-meets-mint shiso character. An aldehyde, so it is the most vulnerable component here: oxidises toward perillic acid and degrades with prolonged heat. Do not boil; infuse warm and covered.
Purple-shiso marker. Less volatile than perillaldehyde, so it holds through cooking and supplies the residual herbal-woody base after the top notes flash off.
D-limonene form. Highly volatile citrus lift; lost quickly to open steam. Also flagged by GC-olfactometry as one of the two most perceptible odorants.
Identified in GC-olfactometry sniffing tests as a predominant perceived odorant despite modest abundance. Ester — hydrolyses under acid or prolonged heat.

Percentage is for GREEN perilla/egoma, where it is dominant; only trace in red/purple shiso. Brings a mushroom-musty note that reads as off-flavour in a sweet dairy base. If sourcing green shiso, expect a materially different and harder-to-place flavour. Also the compound implicated in perilla ketone lung toxicity in grazing livestock (not a concern at culinary leaf doses).
Green-perilla co-marker with perilla ketone. Conjugated enone, oxidation- and heat-sensitive.
Present in both chemotypes as the sesquiterpene backbone; peppery-woody. Very fat-soluble, so it extracts preferentially into cream and persists through freezing.
Co-occurs with beta-caryophyllene; hoppy-woody support note.
Oxidation product of beta-caryophyllene; rises in dried or aged leaf, adding a drier woody-spicy edge. A high proportion signals stale leaf.
Furan monoterpenoid; fresh citrus-herbal lift. Highly volatile — infuse covered or it is lost.
Biosynthetic partner of perillaldehyde in the same terpenoid pathway; oxidises to perillaldehyde. Floral-lilac facet.
Minor floral-lavender contributor.
Sesquiterpene hydrocarbon, LogP 6.4 — partitions almost entirely into the fat phase. Green-woody depth.

shiso.warnings: Leaf colour is the reliable proxy for chemotype: purple/red = perillaldehyde (the flavour most people mean by 'shiso'), green = perilla ketone (mushroom-musty, a different ingredient in practice). Confirm which you have before building a recipe around it. Perilla ketone is a known pulmonary toxin in livestock consuming large quantities of perilla forage; culinary leaf quantities are not a concern. Perilla is also a recognised food allergen for a minority of people.

galangal.name: Galangal
galangal.variety: Greater galangal (the common culinary rhizome). Lesser galangal, Alpinia officinarum, is a distinct species with a different, more pungent profile.
galangal.gcms_summary: Galangal is overwhelmingly a 1,8-cineole ingredient with an ester-driven signature layered on top. GC/GC-MS of A. galanga rhizome oil gives 1,8-cineole 53.4%, beta-sesquiphellandrene 5.9%, chavicol 5.0%, terpinen-4-ol 2.9%, beta-caryophyllene 2.7%, alpha-terpineol 2.1%, eugenyl acetate 1.9%, zingiberenol 1.6%, beta-pinene 1.5% and alpha-pinene 1.1%. Two-dimensional GC-TOF-MS identified 102 compounds (47 hydrocarbons, 25 alcohols, 7 ketones, 7 esters, 3 aldehydes, 4 ethers, 9 other), 42 of them reported in the species for the first time. Aroma extract dilution analysis with GC-olfactometry on fresh rhizome detected 43 odorants at FD factors of 1–4096, elucidated 36 structures, and reconstructed the characteristic aroma from 20 major odorants at natural concentrations. Ranked by odor activity value: 1,8-cineole (OAV ~130,000, eucalyptus-leaf), (S)-galangal acetate (~44,000, fruity-pungent), eugenol (~1,600, clove), chavicol acetate (~980, mushroom), chavicol (~220, phenolic). Stereochemistry matters: only the (S)-enantiomer of acetoxychavicol carries the cool woody ginger-like odor, and of the eight acetoxy-1,8-cineole isomers only trans-2-acetoxy-1,8-cineole gives the woody galanga-like note that was judged the single most important odor constituent. Fresh rhizome reads as eucalyptus-leaf-like, fruity, pungent and floral.

compounds.notes: The defining compound at over half the oil and by far the highest OAV (~130,000). Eucalyptus-camphor-cooling. Volatile cyclic ether — it flashes off in open steam, so infuse covered. Its cooling character is amplified perceptually at frozen serving temperature, so dose conservatively; easy to overshoot into medicinal territory.

Judged the single most characteristic odor constituent of galangal. Only the trans-2 isomer of eight possible acetoxy-1,8-cineoles carries the woody galanga note. Acetate ester — hydrolysis under prolonged heat or acid destroys the specific galanga identity while leaving the generic cineole eucalyptus behind. This is the strongest argument against long, acidic, or high-heat processing.
Second-highest OAV (~44,000), fruity-pungent, cool woody, ginger-like. Only the (S)-enantiomer carries the characteristic odor. Diacetate ester — same hydrolysis vulnerability as above.
Most abundant sesquiterpene. Low volatility and heat-stable; contributes woody-spicy body that survives cooking.
Free phenol, OAV ~220, raw phenolic note. Rises as chavicol acetate hydrolyses, so an over-cooked infusion drifts phenolic-medicinal.
OAV ~980, mushroom-like and earthy. Ester — hydrolyses on prolonged heating to free chavicol, shifting mushroom toward raw phenolic.
OAV ~1,600, clove-like. Phenolic, more water-tolerant than the terpenes here, and stable to heat. Reliably survives custard processing.
Woody-earthy, faintly medicinal; part of the pine-camphor supporting cast.
Lilac-floral softener against the cineole sharpness.
Peppery-woody. Shared with shiso — the main compound overlap between the two ingredients. Very fat-soluble, extracts into cream.
Sweeter, softer clove note than free eugenol. Ester — hydrolyses toward eugenol under heat and acid.
Sesquiterpene alcohol, woody ginger-like. LogP 4.3, low volatility, heat-stable — supplies lingering depth after top notes are gone.
Pine-resinous. Very volatile, lost early.
Pine-turpentine. Very volatile, lost early.

Clove-carnation, spicy-herbal. The sole compound FlavorDB lists for the Alpinia genus entry (entity_id 301). Note methyleugenol is a regulated substance in some jurisdictions due to genotoxicity findings at high doses; culinary galangal levels are not a concern.
Named in the flavor-characteristics work as an important monoterpenoid odor component alongside geranyl acetate. Floral-lavender lift.
Named alongside linalool as an important odor component. Rose-floral, fruity. Ester — heat and acid sensitive.

galangal.warnings: Greater galangal (A. galanga) and lesser galangal (A. officinarum) are different species with different volatile profiles; recipes are not interchangeable. Galangal's flavour is unusually dependent on fragile acetate esters (galangal acetate, trans-2-acetoxy-1,8-cineole, chavicol acetate, eugenyl acetate) whose hydrolysis products are phenolic and generic-eucalyptus — long, hot, or acidic extraction destroys the specific galanga identity rather than merely weakening it. Dried galangal has lost most of the ester layer and is not a substitute for fresh where the aroma is the point. Contains methyleugenol, regulated in some jurisdictions at high doses.
